Definition and safe injection practice

Definition

A safe injection does not harm the recipient, does not expose the provider to any avoidable risk, and does not result in any waste that is dangerous for other people.

Safe injection practice requires the provider to know:

  • the type of injection and the best injection sites (adult and paediatric);
  • the infection control standards;
  • the aseptic technique used in medication preparation;
  • how to deal with a sharp injury if one occurs.

WHO 7 steps for a safe injection

WHO recommends that health care providers focus on seven steps that make every injection safe and avoid the risks of unsafe injections.

Clean workspace
Hand hygiene
Sterile new syringe and needle
Sterile vial and diluent
Skin disinfection
Sharps collection
Waste management

Step 3 uses a syringe and needle with re-use prevention and/or injury protection features whenever possible.

Hand hygiene and gloves

High-yield

Hand hygiene before and after contact with every patient is the single most important means of preventing the spread of infection.

  • Ensure hands are dry before starting any activity.
  • Do not use alcohol-based hand products when hands are visibly soiled. Wash with antibacterial or plain soap and running water, then dry with single-use paper towels.

When to use gloves

Gloves needed

  • Health care worker's skin is non-intact
  • Patient's skin is non-intact
  • Giving an IV injection
  • Exposure to blood is anticipated

Gloves may not be needed

  • SC, IM, or intradermal injections
  • Health care worker's skin is intact
  • Patient's skin is intact

Injection devices

Use a sterile single-use device and a new device for each procedure. Inspect the packaging to make sure the protective barrier is intact. Discard the device if the package is punctured, torn, or damaged by moisture, or if the expiry date has passed.

WHO recommends safety-engineered syringes to ensure safe injection. There are three types:

TypeNameMechanism
SIP Sharp injury protection Sharps-protection feature on single-use hypodermic needles; a mechanism covers the needle after the injection to prevent needle-stick injuries. Includes manual and automatic retractable syringes.
RUP Reuse prevention Sterile single-use syringe with a weak spot in the plunger that makes it break if the user tries to pull back after the injection.
AD Auto disable Named as the third type; the selected pages give no further description.

Medication vials

A multi-dose vial holds liquid medication for parenteral administration (injection or infusion) containing more than one dose. It is labelled as such by the manufacturer and typically contains an antimicrobial preservative to help prevent bacterial growth. If you can, choose a single-dose vial.

If a multidose vial must be used

  • Keep one multidose vial for each patient, stored with the patient's name on it in a separate treatment or medication room.
  • Do not store multidose vials in the open ward, where spray or spatter could contaminate them.
  • Wipe the access diaphragm (septum) with 70% alcohol (isopropyl alcohol or ethanol) on a swab or cotton-wool ball before piercing the vial.

How re-using a syringe spreads infection

The source illustrates this with an HCV-infected patient.

  1. New needle and syringe

    They are used to draw medication.

  2. Backflow

    When used on an HCV-infected patient, backflow contaminates the syringe. Changing the needle does not prevent this.

  3. Vial contaminated

    Re-using the contaminated syringe to obtain medication contaminates the vial.

  4. Other patients infected

    If the vial is used for other patients, they can become infected with HCV.

High-yield

HCV is only the example: the same principles apply to other bloodborne pathogens.

Skin preparation and disinfection

  1. Apply the solution

    Use 60–70% alcohol-based solution (isopropyl alcohol or ethanol) on a single-use swab or cotton-wool ball.

  2. Wipe centre outwards

    Start at the centre of the injection site and work outwards, without going over the same area.

  3. Allow to dry

    Apply for 30 seconds, then let the site dry completely.

Sharps collection and waste management

High-yield

Needles must not be recapped, bent, broken, removed from disposable syringes, or otherwise manipulated by hand.

  • The person who used the sharp is responsible for its immediate safe disposal, preferably at the point of use.
  • Dispose of waste with care.

Check yourself

Which hand-cleaning method is used when hands are visibly soiled?

Antibacterial or plain soap and running water, dried with single-use paper towels. Alcohol-based hand products are not used.

Why does changing the needle not make a used syringe safe to re-use?

Backflow from the injection contaminates the syringe itself, and the contaminated syringe can then contaminate the vial.

How is the skin disinfected before an injection?

With 60–70% alcohol, wiping from the centre outwards without going over the same area, for 30 seconds, then letting it dry completely.

Key Points / Quick Review

Definition

  • No harm to the recipient, no avoidable risk to the provider, no dangerous waste for others.

WHO 7 steps

  • Clean workspace, hand hygiene, sterile new syringe and needle, sterile vial and diluent, skin disinfection, sharps collection, waste management.

Hand hygiene and gloves

  • Hand hygiene before and after every patient is the most important preventive measure.
  • Gloves for non-intact skin, IV injection, or anticipated blood exposure.

Devices

  • New single-use device each time; discard if package is damaged or expired.
  • SIP covers the needle, RUP breaks the plunger on re-use, AD is the third type.

Vials

  • Prefer single-dose vials.
  • Multidose: one per patient, labelled, kept in the treatment room; wipe the septum with 70% alcohol.

Skin, sharps and waste

  • 60–70% alcohol, centre outwards, 30 seconds, dry completely.
  • Never recap or manipulate needles by hand; dispose immediately at the point of use.
